source_text: Communis igitur origo ludorum utriusque generis, communes et tituli, ut de Communibus causis. perinde apparatus communes habeant necesse est de reatu generali idololatriae conditricis suae. sed circensium paulo pompatior suggestus, quibus proprie hoc nomen: pompa praecedens, quorum sit in semetipsa probans de simulacrorum serie, de imaginum agmine, de curribus, de tensis, de armamaxis, de sedibus, de coronis, de exuuiis. quanta praeterea sacra quanta sacrificia praecedant, intercedant, succedant, quot collegia, quot sacerdotia, quot officia moueantur, sciunt homines illius urbis, in qua daemoniorum conuentus consedit. ea si minore cura per prouincias pro minoribus uiribus administrantur, tamen omnes ubique circenses illuc deputandi, unde et petuntur, inde inquirantur, unde sumuntur. nam et riuulus tenuis ex suo fonte et surculus modicus ex sua, fronde qualitatem originis continet. uiderit ambitio siue frugalitas eius ** sit. deum offendit qualiscumque pompa circi: etsi pauca simulacra circumferat, in uno idololatria est; etsi un am tensam trahat, Iouis tamen plaustrum est; quaeuis idololatria sordide instructa uel modice locuples et splendida est censu criminis sui.
thought_title: Common origin and apparatus of the games
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that both sacred and funereal games share one idolatrous origin, and now turns to the common apparatus of the games, especially the more ostentatious parade of the circus.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore the origin of the games of both kinds is common, and the titles are common, as about the common causes. Likewise they must have common apparatus because of the general guilt of idolatry their founder. But the display of the circus is a little more pompous, to which this name properly belongs: the parade going before, proving in itself whose it is, from the row of images, from the procession of statues, from the chariots, from the tensae, from the armamaxae, from the seats, from the crowns, from the spoils. How many sacred rites besides, how many sacrifices go before, come between, follow after, how many colleges, how many priesthoods, how many offices are set in motion, the people of that city know, in which the assembly of demons has settled. If these things are administered with less care in the provinces because of smaller resources, nevertheless all circuses everywhere must be assigned to that place from which they are also sought, let them be traced from that place from which they are taken. For both a thin stream from its own source and a small shoot from its own foliage retains the quality of its origin. Ambition or frugality of it may see to it. Any parade of the circus, of whatever kind, offends God: even if it carries around few images, in one there is idolatry; even if it draws one tensa, nevertheless it is the wagon of Jupiter; any idolatry meanly equipped or moderately rich is also splendid in the wealth of its own crime.

lemmas.gloss: sacred wagon for images of gods

choices.why: Keeps the literal force of the participle as a present active participle describing the parade's action of preceding the games.

choices.term: de simulacrorum serie, de imaginum agmine
choices.english: from the row of images, from the procession of statues
choices.why: Distinguishes simulacra (cult images) from imagines (statues or busts) while preserving the parallel prepositional structure.
rejected: from the series of idols, from the train of images
from the line of effigies, from the column of statues

choices.english: the assembly of demons has settled
choices.why: Conuentus means assembly or gathering; consedit (has settled) conveys the demons' established presence in Rome.

choices.english: a thin stream from its own source
choices.why: Tenuis means thin or slender, and the possessive suo emphasizes the stream's own source, matching the parallel with surculus.
rejected: a small brook from its spring
a slender rivulet from its fountain

choices.english: retains the quality of its origin
choices.why: Qualitas is a technical term for essential character; continet means holds or retains, preserving the metaphor.
rejected: keeps the nature of its source
preserves the character of its beginning

choices.english: in the wealth of its own crime
choices.why: Census means wealth or assessment; the phrase is paradoxical, saying idolatry is rich precisely in its criminality.
rejected: by the assessment of its crime
in the riches of its guilt

pass_b_english: The games of both kinds, then, have a common origin, and their titles are common, since their causes are common. So their apparatus must also be common, because of the general guilt of the idolatry that gave them birth.

But the display of the circus is somewhat more ostentatious, and to it belongs this name in a special sense: the parade that goes before. This parade proves what it is in itself from the row of images, from the procession of statues, from the chariots, the sacred wagons, the covered carriages, the thrones, the crowns, the spoils.

How many sacred rites besides, how many sacrifices go before, come between, and follow after; how many colleges, how many priesthoods, how many offices are set in motion—the people of Rome know, where the assembly of demons has settled.

If these things are administered with less care in the provinces because of smaller resources, still all circuses everywhere must be assigned to that source from which they are sought; let them be traced back to the place from which they are taken. For a thin stream from its own source, and a modest shoot from its own foliage, retains the quality of its origin.

Let ambition or frugality see to what the parade's character is. Any parade of the circus, whatever its quality, offends God: even if it carries around few images, in one there is idolatry; even if it draws one sacred wagon, it is still Jupiter's chariot. Any idolatry, however meanly equipped or modestly wealthy, is splendid in the wealth of its own crime.
notes: The source text contains a lacuna marked by '**' after 'eius' in the clause 'uiderit ambitio siue frugalitas eius ** sit'; the gloss renders what is present without inventing the missing word.

polish.changed: Clarified that 'that city' is Rome, resolved the ambiguous 'its' in the ambition/frugality sentence by naming the parade, and broke up long sentences for easier reading aloud while preserving every claim and qualification.

notes.quote: Let ambition or frugality see to what its character is
notes.why: Ambition and frugality personified as agents; unclear what 'its' refers to (the parade's character?).
notes.fix: Recast: 'Whether ambitious or frugal, each parade retains its origin's character'.

notes.quote: the people of that city know
notes.why: 'That city' = Rome, but vague; reader may not connect to Rome specifically.

notes.quote: they also call the Luperci ludii
notes.why: 'ludii' is introduced as the Latin term for games/performers but then English 'games' is used without signposting, so the reader loses the Latin thread.
notes.fix: Define 'ludii' once as 'games/performers' and then use 'games' consistently.
